title: Dropout as a Bayesian Approximation:  Representing Model Uncertainty in Deep Learning
Dropout as a Bayesian Approximation: Representing Model Uncertainty in Deep Learning
summary: Deep learning regression and classification tools typically do not capture model uncertainty, whereas Bayesian models do but at prohibitive computational cost. The paper casts dropout training in neural networks as approximate variational inference in deep Gaussian processes, yielding MC dropout: averaging T stochastic forward passes to estimate predictive mean and variance. On UCI regression benchmarks, notably Boston Housing, MC dropout improves test RMSE and predictive log-likelihood over VI and probabilistic back-propagation, achieving 2.97 ± 0.19 RMSE on Boston Housing in the 20-split setting.

text: Cloning into 'repo'...

why: The authors' repo is cloned and contains the entire experimental apparatus: experiment.py, net/net.py, and all UCI_Datasets directories with data.txt, the exact 20 train/test index splits, dropout_rates.txt, tau_values.txt, n_epochs/n_hidden configs, plus the authors' published result files (test_MC_rmse_100_xepochs_1_hidden_layers.txt etc.) for direct comparison. Nothing data- or weight-wise is missing (models are trained from scratch). What is broken is the runtime: the code targets Keras 2.2.0 on Theano 0.8.2 (README), Theano is unmaintained and not installable on Python 3.12, TF1.x/Keras 2.2 wheels do not exist for Python 3.12, and 9 of 11 Python files are Python-2 style. So we keep the authors' logic (architecture, dropout rates, epochs, tau/grid-search protocol, per-split train/val selection) but port the training/evaluation core to a modern framework and run the same splits.
est_runtime: Port work: ~20-30 min (rewrite net/net.py + experiment.py training/MC-dropout loop in a modern framework, keep split loading and grid-search logic). Runs (Boston Housing, 1x50 net, 400 epochs, batch 32, per-split grid over the repo's dropout_rates/tau_values, T MC forward passes): ~10-15 s per model fit on 22 CPU cores, so ~2-4 min per split with grid search. Full 20-split C1 protocol is ~40-80 min of compute, i.e. borderline-to-over the ~60 min total budget once the port is included.
scale_down_plan: Keep the exact released protocol but shrink along the split axis, not the model axis: evaluate the first 5 of the 20 released Boston Housing splits (index_train_*/index_test_*), same 1-hidden-layer/50-unit net, same dropout rates, same l=1e-2, same per-split train/val grid over tau, same 10x epochs (400), batch 32, Adam, T MC forward passes. Report mean test RMSE with standard error over 5 splits and state the split count explicitly. Secondary cheap confirmation on Yacht Hydrodynamics (N=308, <1 min/split) if time permits. Expected effect on the number: the point estimate should land near the released 2.83-2.97 range within a much wider error bar (SE roughly sqrt(20/5)~2x larger, i.e. +/-0.3-0.4 instead of +/-0.19); the qualitative claim (MC dropout beats VI, comparable-to-better than PBP 3.01) remains testable, but the printed +/-0.19 cannot be matched with 5 splits. If the port finishes fast, extend toward 10-20 splits; do not cut epochs or MC samples first, since those change the estimator itself.
blockers: code targets Theano 0.8.2 + Keras 2.2.0; Theano is dead and cannot be installed on Python 3.12
Keras 2.2.0 / TensorFlow 1.x have no wheels for Python 3.12 (and Keras 3 API differs: layer-level train-time dropout loops, .compile/.fit behaviour, model saving)
9 of 11 python files are Python-2 style (print statements, old import style) and need 2to3-style edits even before framework porting
no GPU on this machine; README launch command assumes device=gpu + float32 (not fatal: the UCI nets are tiny and the paper reports CPU-class runtimes, e.g. naval 276 s/split incl. BO)
protocol requires a per-split train/val split + grid search over dropout rate and tau before the final train, so per-split cost is much larger than a single 400-epoch fit

approach: This is a partial_release reproduction: we keep the authors' released data and the exact 20 per-split train/test index files from https://github.com/yaringal/DropoutUncertaintyExps (bostonHousing/data/data.txt, index_train_i.txt, index_test_i.txt, dropout_rates.txt, tau_values.txt, n_epochs.txt, n_hidden.txt) and their grid-search-over-dropout-rate-and-tau protocol, but re-implement the 1-hidden-layer/50-unit dropout network plus the MC-dropout training/evaluation loop in PyTorch (CPU) because the original Keras 2.2.0 + Theano 0.8.2 stack and its Python-2 source cannot run on Python 3.12 (this is the single documented deviation from R13). For each of the first 5 of the 20 released Boston Housing splits we carve an 80/20 train/validation split from the training indices, grid-search dropout rate and tau by validation log-likelihood, set the L2 weight decay from the searched tau and l=1e-2 via the eq.(7) relation exactly as coded in net/net.py, train the final model for the fixed epoch budget (10x the base schedule, ~400 epochs, no early stopping) with Adam/batch-32, and evaluate test RMSE (inverse-transformed to original target units) and predictive log-likelihood with T=1000 MC-dropout stochastic forward passes. reproduce.py aggregates mean±standard-error over the 5 splits, writes results/metrics.json, and prints the authors' released per-split result files for direct comparison. The expected point estimate is ~2.83-2.97 (inside the 0.19 tolerance around C1=2.97) but with a roughly 2x wider standard error (5 of 20 splits), so the honest verdict is partially_reproduced.
steps: 1. Environment: verify python>=3.12, numpy/scipy/pandas/scikit-learn present, then `pip install torch --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu` (CPU wheel) and `python -c "import torch;print(torch.__version__)"`. Do NOT attempt to install Theano/Keras 2.2/TF1 - they are uninstallable on 3.12 (documented blocker; deviation from R13).

2. Repo check: confirm DropoutUncertaintyExps/ is present; assert existence of UCI_Datasets/bostonHousing/data/{data.txt, index_features.txt, index_target.txt, dropout_rates.txt, tau_values.txt, n_epochs.txt, n_hidden.txt, n_splits.txt} and index_train_0..19.txt / index_test_0..19.txt, plus results/ releasing test_MC_rmse_100_xepochs_1_hidden_layers.txt.

3. Read experiment.py and net/net.py end-to-end; write down (in a notes file or docstring) the exact protocol: how the 80/20 train-val split is formed, how (dropout_rate, tau) are grid-searched and scored, how weight decay lambda is derived from tau/l/N, the exact epoch count and multiplier, and how RMSE and eq.(8) log-likelihood are computed. This dictation of the authors' logic is what the PyTorch port must mirror.
4. Parse the bostonHousing data dir config files and print them (dropout rates, tau values, n_epochs, n_hidden, n_splits, index_features, index_target) so the counts drive the grid size.
5. Write config.py with the values above (paper/assumption tags inline).
6. Write data_utils.py: load_data(split) -> (X_train, y_train, X_val, y_val, X_test, y_test, scaler_y); standardize X and y on train statistics; verbose shapes. No torch import needed here.
7. Write model.py: DropoutRegressor(Q, hidden=50, p_in, p_out) with dropout before each weight layer; keep_dropout_at_eval flag.

8. Write mc_dropout.py: compute_lambda(tau,l,N) reading net/net.py's formula; train_model(...) (Adam lr=1e-3, batch 32, fixed epochs, shuffled); mc_predict(model, X, T=1000) -> mean, variance; rmse_inverse(y, yhat_mean, scaler_y); predictive_log_likelihood(...) per eq.(8)/net.py; grid_search(...) scoring by validation LL.

9. Write reproduce.py: iterate config.full_split_list, run grid search then final train then MC test eval, store per-split results, compute mean and SE = std/sqrt(n), set within_tolerance = |mean - 2.97| <= 0.19, dump results/metrics.json including split count, config snapshot, and the authors' released values.
10. Write compare_with_released.py to read the authors' results/*_100_xepochs_1_hidden_layers.txt files and print alongside ours.
11. Run the intermediate checks (see intermediate_checks) and fix any that fail before the full run.
12. Smoke test: `python reproduce.py --smoke` (split 0, 2 epochs, T=10, 1 grid point, 64 samples) - assert finite RMSE/LL, correct tensor shapes, <60 s.
13. Full run: `python reproduce.py --dataset bostonHousing --split-count 5` -> 5 splits x (grid search + 10x-epoch final train + T=1000 MC eval).
14. Inspect results/metrics.json: mean RMSE vs 2.97 with tolerance 0.19; compare to the authors' released 2.83/2.90; confirm the printed SE is ~2x the paper's because only 5 of 20 splits are used.
15. If budget remains after the 5-split Boston run, add a cheap secondary confirmation on Yacht Hydrodynamics (N=308), same protocol, and append it to metrics.json.

16. Write a short summary block into results/metrics.json stating the deviation (5/20 splits, grid-search instead of BO, PyTorch instead of Keras/Theano) and the resulting verdict (partially_reproduced).
smoke_test: `python reproduce.py --smoke` runs only split 0 on the first 64 training rows for 2 epochs with T=10 MC forward passes and a single (dropout,tau) grid point; it asserts the data loader returns correctly shaped train/val/test arrays, the net has 751 parameters, training losses are finite and decreasing, MC predictions have shape (n_test,) with non-negative variance, and RMSE/log-likelihood are finite scalars. It writes results/smoke_metrics.json and must finish in under ~60 s, proving the full data->train->MC-eval->JSON flow before the expensive run.
intermediate_checks: Data integrity: data.txt has 506 rows and Q columns equal to index_features.txt; index_train_i.txt and index_test_i.txt are disjoint and their union is all 506 indices; every index is in range.
Split hygiene: the 80/20 validation set is drawn only from training indices, disjoint from the test indices, and reproducible from the fixed seed (A3/A8).
Grid files parse: dropout_rates.txt and tau_values.txt yield the expected number of values (print them); grid size = len(rates)*len(taus).
Parameter count: 13*50+50 + 50*1+1 = 751 parameters; print and assert this matches the instantiated model.

Weight-decay sanity: print lambda for the searched tau values and N=train size; assert lambda > 0 and varies monotonically with tau as eq.(7)/net.py implies; verify lambda matches net/net.py's formula on a hand-computed example.
Target scaling: after standardization the train target has mean~0, std~1; inverse_transform(standardize(y))==y within 1e-8.

Sanity baseline: fit a plain (dropout-off at eval, or a least-squares linear) model on split 0 and confirm test RMSE is in a plausible Boston range (~3-6), i.e. the pipeline is not degenerate before the dropout run.

Authors' anchor: read UCI_Datasets/bostonHousing/results/test_MC_rmse_100_xepochs_1_hidden_layers.txt and record the released per-split RMSEs (expect point estimate ~2.83-2.97) so our numbers can be compared immediately after the full run.
budget_plan: Total ~60 min. Setup + reading experiment.py/net.py + writing the PyTorch port: ~15-20 min. Intermediate checks: ~5 min. Smoke test: ~1-2 min. Full 5-split Boston Housing run (grid search + 400-epoch final train + T=1000 MC eval, ~2-4 min/split on the CPU cores): ~10-20 min. Aggregation, comparison to released files, and writing results/metrics.json: ~5 min. Remaining ~5-10 min reserved as buffer; if the port finished fast and the buffer is intact, extend the split list toward 10 before considering any reduction of epochs or T (the route forbids shrinking the estimator).

args.content:
"""Data loading for the authors' released UCI_Datasets directories (R10, R11).

Mirrors repo/experiment.py:
  * data.txt holds all columns; index_features.txt / index_target.txt select X / y.
  * index_train_{i}.txt / index_test_{i}.txt are the released random splits
    (disjoint, covering all N rows).
  * The validation set is the LAST 20% of the split's training indices
    (experiment.py: X_validation = X_train[int(0.8*N):] -- deterministic, the
    index files are already random permutations).
Standardisation statistics are always computed on the data the network is
actually trained on (train-val subset during grid search, full train set for
the final fit), exactly as net.py's constructor does with normalize=True.
"""
from dataclasses import dataclass
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np


@dataclass
class SplitData:
    X_train: np.ndarray       # train-val subset (first 80% of train indices)
    y_train: np.ndarray
    X_val: np.ndarray         # validation subset (last 20% of train indices)
    y_val: np.ndarray
    X_train_full: np.ndarray  # full training set (train-val + validation)
    y_train_full: np.ndarray
    X_test: np.ndarray
    y_test: np.ndarray


def _load_int_index(path: Path) -> np.ndarray:
    return np.atleast_1d(np.loadtxt(path)).astype(int)


def read_grid_files(dataset_dir: Path):
    """Read the authors' hyperparameter grid files (verbatim)."""
    data_dir = dataset_dir / "data"
    rates = np.atleast_1d(np.loadtxt(data_dir / "dropout_rates.txt")).astype(float).tolist()
    taus = np.atleast_1d(np.loadtxt(data_dir / "tau_values.txt")).astype(float).tolist()
    n_epochs = int(np.loadtxt(data_dir / "n_epochs.txt"))
    n_hidden = int(np.loadtxt(data_dir / "n_hidden.txt"))
    n_splits = int(np.loadtxt(data_dir / "n_splits.txt"))
    return rates, taus, n_epochs, n_hidden, n_splits


def load_dataset(dataset_dir: Path):
    data_dir = dataset_dir / "data"
    data = np.loadtxt(data_dir / "data.txt")
    index_features = _load_int_index(data_dir / "index_features.txt")
    index_target = int(np.loadtxt(data_dir / "index_target.txt"))
    X = data[:, index_features]
    y = data[:, index_target]
    return X, y


def load_split(dataset_dir: Path, split: int, val_fraction: float = 0.2) -> SplitData:
    X, y = load_dataset(dataset_dir)
    data_dir = dataset_dir / "data"
    index_train = _load_int_index(data_dir / f"index_train_{split}.txt")
    index_test = _load_int_index(data_dir / f"index_test_{split}.txt")

    X_train_full = X[index_train]
    y_train_full = y[index_train]
    X_test = X[index_test]
    y_test = y[index_test]

    # experiment.py lines 132-136: last 20% of the training indices = validation
    num_training = int((1.0 - val_fraction) * X_train_full.shape[0])
    X_train = X_train_full[:num_training]
    y_train = y_train_full[:num_training]
    X_val = X_train_full[num_training:]
    y_val = y_train_full[num_training:]

    return SplitData(X_train, y_train, X_val, y_val,
                     X_train_full, y_train_full, X_test, y_test)


def verify_split_integrity(dataset_dir: Path, n_splits: int) -> dict:
    """Intermediate check: splits are disjoint, cover all rows, indices in range."""
    X, _ = load_dataset(dataset_dir)
    n = X.shape[0]
    all_idx = set(range(n))
    info = {"n_rows": n, "ok": True, "split_sizes": []}
    for i in range(n_splits):
        data_dir = dataset_dir / "data"
        tr = set(_load_int_index(data_dir / f"index_train_{i}.txt").tolist())
        te = set(_load_int_index(data_dir / f"index_test_{i}.txt").tolist())
        if tr & te:
            info["ok"] = False
            info.setdefault("problems", []).append(f"split {i}: train/test overlap")
        if tr | te != all_idx:
            info["ok"] = False
            info.setdefault("problems", []).append(f"split {i}: union != all rows")
        if (min(tr | te) < 0) or (max(tr | te) >= n):
            info["ok"] = False

"""PyTorch port of the authors' Keras dropout regression net (net/net.py).

Architecture for the Table-1 experiments (R1, R2):
    Input -> Dropout(p) -> Dense(50, relu) -> Dropout(p) -> Dense(1)

Details mirrored from net.py / Keras 2.2:
  * Dropout is applied BEFORE every weight layer and is ACTIVE AT TEST TIME
    (net.py builds the graph with Dropout(dropout)(..., training=True)).
    We reproduce this with an explicit `mc` flag so MC forward passes keep
    dropout on while the "standard" prediction runs with dropout off.
  * Keras (inverted) dropout at train time zeroes units with prob p and
    scales the rest by 1/(1-p) -- identical to torch's F.dropout(training=True).
  * Dense default init = Glorot uniform weights, zero biases.
"""
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F


class DropoutRegressor(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, n_features: int, n_hidden: int = 50, p_drop: float = 0.05):
        super().__init__()
        self.p_drop = float(p_drop)
        self.fc1 = nn.Linear(n_features, n_hidden)
        self.fc2 = nn.Linear(n_hidden, 1)
        nn.init.xavier_uniform_(self.fc1.weight)   # Keras glorot_uniform
        nn.init.zeros_(self.fc1.bias)
        nn.init.xavier_uniform_(self.fc2.weight)
        nn.init.zeros_(self.fc2.bias)

    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor, mc: bool = False) -> torch.Tensor:
        training = self.training or mc
        x = F.dropout(x, p=self.p_drop, training=training)   # before weight layer 1
        x = F.relu(self.fc1(x))
        x = F.dropout(x, p=self.p_drop, training=training)   # before weight layer 2
        return self.fc2(x)


def count_parameters(model: nn.Module) -> int:
    return sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters())

args.content:
"""Core MC-dropout logic, a faithful PyTorch port of repo/net/net.py.

net.py essentials that are reproduced 1:1:
  * normalize=True: standardise X (std with ddof=0, zero-std -> 1) and y on the
    statistics of the data the net is trained on; predictions are inverse
    transformed to original target units before RMSE / log-likelihood.
  * L2 weight decay per kernel: reg = lengthscale**2 * (1 - dropout) /
    (2. * N * tau)  with N = size of the data the net is trained on (R3, eq. 7).
  * loss = mean_squared_error + reg * (||W1||^2 + ||W2||^2)   (biases exempt)
  * Adam (lr 1e-3, betas 0.9/0.999, eps 1e-7), fixed epoch count, per-epoch
    shuffled mini-batches, no early stopping (R5, R6, R12).
  * predict(): deterministic "standard" RMSE (dropout off), MC RMSE from the
    mean of T=10000 stochastic forward passes (R8, eq. 6), and predictive
    log-likelihood per eq. (8) (R9) using the net's tau on the original scale.
"""
import time
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

import numpy as np
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F
from scipy.special import logsumexp

import config
from model import DropoutRegressor


def weight_decay_reg(tau: float, dropout: float, n_train: int,
                     lengthscale: float = config.LENGTHSCALE) -> float:
    """net.py line 72: reg = lengthscale**2 * (1 - dropout) / (2. * N * tau)."""
    return lengthscale**2 * (1.0 - dropout) / (2.0 * n_train * tau)


class MC dropoutNet:  # noqa: N801 - intentionally mirrors net.py's `net`
    """Port of net.py's class net (constructor trains the model)."""

    def __init__(self, X_train, y_train, n_hidden=50, n_epochs=400,
                 tau=1.0, dropout=0.05, batch_size=config.BATCH_SIZE,
                 seed=0, verbose=False):
        X_train = np.asarray(X_train, dtype=np.float32)
        y_train = np.asarray(y_train, dtype=np.float32)

        # --- normalisation (net.py: normalize=True branch) -----------------
        self.std_X = X_train.std(axis=0)
        self.std_X[self.std_X == 0] = 1.0
        self.mean_X = X_train.mean(axis=0)
        self.mean_y = float(y_train.mean())
        self.std_y = float(y_train.std())
        Xn = (X_train - self.mean_X) / self.std_X
        yn = ((y_train - self.mean_y) / self.std_y).reshape(-1, 1)

        self.tau = float(tau)
        self.dropout = float(dropout)
        N = Xn.shape[0]
        self.reg = weight_decay_reg(tau, dropout, N)

        torch.manual_seed(seed)
        self.model = DropoutRegressor(Xn.shape[1], n_hidden=n_hidden, p_drop=dropout)
        opt = torch.optim.Adam(self.model.parameters(), lr=config.ADAM_LR,
                               betas=config.ADAM_BETAS, eps=config.ADAM_EPS)

        Xt = torch.from_numpy(Xn)
        yt = torch.from_numpy(yn)
        gen = torch.Generator().manual_seed(seed)

        start = time.time()
        for _ in range(int(n_epochs)):
            self.model.train()
            perm = torch.randperm(N, generator=gen)
            for i in range(0, N, batch_size):
                idx = perm[i:i + batch_size]
                pred = self.model(Xt[idx])
                mse = F.mse_loss(pred, yt[idx])  # mean over batch (Keras MSE)
                l2 = self.reg * (self.model.fc1.weight.pow(2).sum()
                                 + self.model.fc2.weight.pow(2).sum())
                loss = mse + l2
                opt.zero_grad()
                loss.backward()
                opt.step()
        self.running_time = time.time() - start
        if verbose:
            print(f"    trained net: N={N} tau={tau} p={dropout} reg={self.reg:.3e} "
                  f"epochs={n_epochs} time={self.running_time:.1f}s")

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    def _forward_scaled(self, X, mc, T=1):
        """Forward passes returning predictions on the ORIGINAL target scale.

        mc=False: single deterministic pass (dropout off) -> (n,).
        mc=True : T stochastic passes -> (T, n); rows get independent masks
                  (A27: equivalent in expectation to net.py's T loop).
        """
        Xn = (np.asarray(X, dtype=np.float32) - self.mean_X) / self.std_X
        Xt = torch.from_numpy(Xn)
        self.model.eval()
        with torch.no_grad():
            if not mc:
                out = self.model(Xt, mc=False).squeeze(1).numpy()
                return out * self.std_y + self.mean_y
            n = Xt.shape[0]
            reps_per_chunk = max(1, config.MC_CHUNK_ROWS // max(n, 1))
            chunks = []
            done = 0
            while done < T:
                r = min(reps_per_chunk, T - done)
                Xr = Xt.repeat(r, 1)
                pr = self.model(Xr, mc=True).squeeze(1)  # (r*n,)
                chunks.append(pr.view(r, n).numpy())
                done += r
            Yt = np.concatenate(chunks, axis=0)          # (T, n)
        return Yt * self.std_y + self.mean_y

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    def predict(self, X_test, y_test, T=config.N_MC_SAMPLES):
        """Port of net.py predict(): (standard_rmse, MC_rmse, test_ll)."""
        y_test = np.asarray(y_test, dtype=np.float64)

        standard_pred = self._forward_scaled(X_test, mc=False)
        rmse_standard = float(np.sqrt(np.mean((y_test - standard_pred) ** 2)))

        Yt_hat = self._forward_scaled(X_test, mc=True, T=T)  # (T, n) original scale
        MC_pred = Yt_hat.mean(axis=0)
        rmse_mc = float(np.sqrt(np.mean((y_test - MC_pred) ** 2)))

        # eq. (8): log p ~ logsumexp_t(-0.5*tau*(y - y_t)^2) - log T
        #                - 0.5*log(2*pi) + 0.5*log(tau);   mean over test points
        ll = (logsumexp(-0.5 * self.tau * (y_test[None, :] - Yt_hat) ** 2, axis=0)
              - np.log(Yt_hat.shape[0])
              - 0.5 * np.log(2 * np.pi)
              + 0.5 * np.log(self.tau))
        test_ll = float(np.mean(ll))
        return rmse_standard, rmse_mc, test_ll

import re
import time

import numpy as np
import torch

import config

import mc_dropout
from model import DropoutRegressor

def parse_claim_target():
    """Pull the C1 target value/tolerance out of the provided claim contract."""
    try:
        contract = json.loads(Path("state/claim_contract.json").read_text())
        for claim in contract.get("claims", []):
            if claim.get("id") == "C1":
                m = re.search(r"is\s+([0-9.]+)\s*±\s*([0-9.]+)", claim["statement"])
                if m:
                    return float(m.group(1)), float(m.group(2))
    except Exception as e:  # contract check is optional, never fatal
        print(f"(could not parse claim contract target: {e})")
    return None, None

    print(f"  model parameters: {n_params} (expected 751)")

    # 3. weight-decay formula sanity vs hand computation (net.py line 72)
    l, p, N, tau = 1e-2, 0.05, 364, 0.2
    hand = (l * l) * (1 - p) / (2.0 * N * tau)
    got = mc_dropout.weight_decay_reg(tau=tau, dropout=p, n_train=N, lengthscale=l)
    assert abs(hand - got) < 1e-15 and got > 0

    # 4. target standardisation round-trip
    rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

args.content:
"""Print our per-split results next to the authors' released result files.

The released files (repo/UCI_Datasets/<name>/results/*_100_xepochs_1_hidden_layers.txt)
are the authors' own grid-search run at 100x40=4000 epochs; our run uses the
paper Table-1 budget of 10x40=400 epochs. Values from the released files are
read from disk, never hardcoded.
"""
import json
import math
import sys
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np

import config


def main(dataset="bostonHousing"):
    dataset_dir = config.DATASET_DIRS[dataset]
    rdir = dataset_dir / "results"
    rel_rmse = np.atleast_1d(np.loadtxt(rdir / "test_MC_rmse_100_xepochs_1_hidden_layers.txt"))
    rel_ll = np.atleast_1d(np.loadtxt(rdir / "test_ll_100_xepochs_1_hidden_layers.txt"))
    rel_tau = np.atleast_1d(np.loadtxt(rdir / "test_tau_100_xepochs_1_hidden_layers.txt"))

    ours = json.loads((config.RESULTS_DIR / "metrics.json").read_text())
    our_rmse = np.array(ours["per_split_mc_rmse"])
    our_ll = np.array(ours["per_split_test_ll"])
    our_tau = np.array(ours["per_split_best_tau"])
    n = len(our_rmse)

    print(f"dataset: {dataset}")
    print(f"{'split':>5} | {'ours MC rmse':>12} | {'released MC rmse':>16} | "
          f"{'ours ll':>8} | {'released ll':>11} | {'ours tau':>8} | {'rel tau':>7}")
    for i in range(n):
        print(f"{i:>5} | {our_rmse[i]:>12.4f} | {rel_rmse[i]:>16.4f} | "
              f"{our_ll[i]:>8.4f} | {rel_ll[i]:>11.4f} | {our_tau[i]:>8} | {rel_tau[i]:>7}")
    print(f"\nours:     mean MC rmse {our_rmse.mean():.4f} +- "
          f"{our_rmse.std()/math.sqrt(n):.4f} (SE), mean ll {our_ll.mean():.4f}  ({n} splits, 400 epochs)")
    m = len(rel_rmse)
    print(f"released: mean MC rmse {rel_rmse.mean():.4f} +- "
          f"{rel_rmse.std()/math.sqrt(m):.4f} (SE), mean ll {rel_ll.mean():.4f}  ({m} splits, 4000 epochs)")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main(sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "bostonHousing")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Secondary configuration: the ORIGINAL 2015 paper protocol (commit a6259f1,
# bostonHousing/net/net/net.py + experiment.py). It trains directly on the
# full train set (no validation split) with fixed dropout p=0.05 and the
# BO-found model precision tau=0.159707652696 hardcoded in that file, at
# n_epochs*10 = 400 epochs and batch_size=128. tau is an INPUT hyperparameter
# taken from the authors' original source (their experiment_BO.py output);
# the authors later flagged this shared-tau scheme for test-set contamination
# and replaced it with the per-split grid search used in our primary run.
PAPER2015_TAU = 0.159707652696
PAPER2015_DROPOUT = 0.05


def run_fixed_protocol(dataset_dir, n_splits, tau, dropout, batch_size,
                       n_epochs, T, seed_base, label):
    """Original-paper-style run: fixed (tau, dropout), no grid search,
    trained on the full train set of each released split."""
    print(f"--- secondary config [{label}]: fixed tau={tau} p={dropout} "
          f"batch={batch_size} epochs={n_epochs} ---")
    per_split, per_split_std, per_split_ll, secs = [], [], [], []
    for split in range(n_splits):
        sd = data_utils.load_split(dataset_dir, split)
        net = mc_dropout.MCDropoutNet(sd.X_train_full, sd.y_train_full,
                                      n_epochs=n_epochs, tau=tau, dropout=dropout,
                                      batch_size=batch_size,
                                      seed=seed_base + 1000 * split)
        rs, rm, ll = net.predict(sd.X_test, sd.y_test, T=T)
        per_split.append(rm); per_split_std.append(rs); per_split_ll.append(ll)
        secs.append(net.running_time)
        print(f"  split {split}: MC rmse={rm:.4f} standard rmse={rs:.4f} ll={ll:.4f}")
    mc = np.array(per_split); lls = np.array(per_split_ll)
    n = len(mc)
    out = {
        "label": label,
        "mean_mc_rmse": float(mc.mean()),
        "std_error": float(mc.std() / math.sqrt(n)),
        "per_split_mc_rmse": mc.tolist(),
        "per_split_standard_rmse": per_split_std,
        "mean_test_ll": float(lls.mean()),
        "test_ll_std_error": float(lls.std() / math.sqrt(n)),
        "tau": tau, "dropout": dropout, "batch_size": batch_size,
        "n_epochs": n_epochs, "n_splits": n,
        "seconds": float(sum(secs)),
    }
    print(f"  [{label}] mean MC rmse {out['mean_mc_rmse']:.4f} +- "
          f"{out['std_error']:.4f} (SE), mean ll {out['mean_test_ll']:.4f}, "
          f"{sum(secs):.0f}s")
    return out

    t0=time.time()
    net = mc_dropout.MCDropoutNet(sd.X_train, sd.y_train, n_epochs=400, tau=0.15, dropout=0.05, batch_size=128, seed=7)
    t1=time.time()
    net.predict(sd.X_val, sd.y_val)
